intro: Most of the Bible tells a story or gives a law. This unit turns to the books that sing and the books that argue. The Psalms are 150 poems that have been sung in synagogues and churches for more than two thousand years. The wisdom books, Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, ask plain questions: How should I live? Why do good people suffer? Does anything last? What is love?

You will read these books closely, in translation. You will learn how Hebrew poetry works, with its paired lines and its pictures from daily life. You will sort the psalms by type, meet an Egyptian text that resembles Proverbs, follow the argument in Job to the storm at its end, and see why Jewish and Christian readers have read a love poem as something more.

By the end you will be able to name the pattern in a Hebrew poem, tell a lament from a hymn, explain how different traditions have used these texts, and write a psalm-shaped poem of your own. Everything here is the study of a text and its readers. Nobody is asked to believe or disbelieve; everyone is asked to read carefully.
bigQuestion: What happens when a tradition keeps poems and arguments that do not agree, and keeps singing them?

timeline.t: The Instruction of Amenemope is composed in Egypt, an advice book later compared with Proverbs
The time of David, the king tradition names on seventy-three psalms
King Hezekiah's men copy out sayings of Solomon, as Proverbs 25:1 says
Babylon destroys Jerusalem; Psalm 137 remembers the exile
Ecclesiastes is written, in the view of most scholars
The collection of 150 psalms is largely complete, in the view of many scholars
Rabbi Akiva defends the Song of Songs as the holy of holies among the Writings
The Mishnah records the psalm the Levites sang each day in the Temple
Gregorian chant of the psalms is written down in Christian monasteries
The Genevan Psalter puts rhymed psalms in the mouths of whole congregations
Robert Lowth names parallelism in his lectures on Hebrew poetry
Thomas A. Dorsey writes "Take My Hand, Precious Lord" in Chicago

words.d: the main pattern of Hebrew poetry: a line is followed by a second line that repeats, sharpens or answers it
a psalm type that cries out in trouble, asks for help and often ends in trust; the largest group
a psalm type that calls people to honor God and gives reasons; also called a hymn
the heading above a psalm, which may name a person, a tune, an instrument or an occasion
a poem whose lines or sections begin with the letters of the alphabet in order, such as Psalm 119
Psalms 113 to 118, a set of praise psalms sung at Jewish festivals such as Passover
biblical books, mainly Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes, that ask how to live well and reason from experience
a short, memorable saying that states a lesson drawn from experience
the belief that God rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life, so suffering must be deserved
Hebrew for breath, vapor or mist; the key word of Ecclesiastes, translated vanity in the King James Version
reading a story or poem as a picture of something else, such as the Song of Songs as the love of God and Israel
the list of books a community counts as its scripture

test.q: How many psalms are in the Book of Psalms, and in how many books are they arranged?
test.why: The 150 psalms are arranged in five books, each ending with a doxology.

test.q: Which psalm type is the largest group?
test.why: Laments, cries for help that often end in trust, outnumber every other type.

test.q: "The LORD is my shepherd" opens which psalm?
test.why: Psalm 23 begins with the shepherd image and ends with a host setting a table.

test.q: In Hebrew poetry, what usually follows a line?
choices: A line of exactly ten syllables
A second line that repeats, sharpens or answers it
test.why: That pairing is parallelism, the basic pattern of the psalms and Proverbs.

test.q: How does the JPS Tanakh of 1917 begin Psalm 1, where the King James Version has "Blessed"?
test.why: Both translate the Hebrew ashrei; JPS 1917 chose "Happy is the man."

choices: The exile in Babylon after 586 BCE
The crossing of the Red Sea
test.why: "By the rivers of Babylon" places the psalm among the exiles after Jerusalem's fall.

test.q: Which of these is true about the heading "A Psalm of David"?
choices: It was added by the King James translators.
Tradition reads it as authorship; many scholars read it as collection or style.
It proves the psalm was written in Greek.
test.why: The Hebrew le-David allows more than one reading, and the two kinds of readers differ.

test.q: Which book has a section, Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22, that resembles the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope?
test.why: The "words of the wise" in Proverbs share sayings and images with Amenemope.

test.q: What does Proverbs 1:7 call the beginning of knowledge?
test.why: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" is the book's motto, repeated in Proverbs 9:10.

test.q: What belief do Job's three friends defend?
choices: That love is strong as death
That the psalms should be sung daily
test.why: The friends hold retribution theology: the good prosper and the wicked suffer, so Job must have sinned.

test.q: What does God's speech from the whirlwind consist of?
test.why: Job 38–41 asks Job where he was at creation and describes wild creatures; it never explains his suffering.

test.q: Which English word did the King James Version choose for the Hebrew hevel in Ecclesiastes?
test.why: The KJV reads "Vanity of vanities." The Hebrew means breath or vapor.

test.q: How has Jewish tradition read the Song of Songs?
choices: As the love between God and Israel
As a record of Solomon's marriages
As a set of Temple laws
test.why: Rabbinic tradition, following Rabbi Akiva, read the Song as an allegory of God and Israel and reads it at Passover.

test.q: In which Jewish practice is Proverbs 31:10 to 31 used?
choices: Sung at the Sabbath table on Friday night
test.why: Eshet Chayil, the woman of valor, is traditionally sung as the Sabbath begins.

test.q: Which Chicago figure is often called the father of gospel music?
test.why: Dorsey led the choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church and wrote "Take My Hand, Precious Lord" in 1932.

write.prompt: Do the wisdom books agree about how life works? Cite Proverbs 15:1 or 22:6, Job 38:4 and Ecclesiastes 1:2. Explain what each passage says, how the three fit or clash, and how at least one Jewish or Christian reader has handled the tension.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you cite a passage.
Say who holds each view: the text, Jewish tradition, Christian readers or scholars.
Compare the passages; do not decide which one is true.
Use the unit's terms: parallelism, proverb, retribution theology, hevel.
Quote only short lines, and say which translation you used.
